title: Reinforced Fast Weights via Next-Sequence Prediction
claim: Token-level next-token supervision mismatches recurrent-memory models; sequence-level rollout rewards cut output drift relative to standard training.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; architecture diagram, NTP vs ours comparison, drift plots
description: Three bordered panels, read left to right. (a) shows the fast weight architecture: rows of orange token blocks at the bottom and top, with rounded blue Apply and Update boxes between them. A blue W enters from the left, and Q and K,V arrows feed the boxes. (b) compares Standard NTP (baseline) with ReFINE (ours). The NTP half has rows for input, predicted, ground truth and per-position cross-entropy loss. The ReFINE half adds an entropy bar with a highlighted high-entropy position, then multi-token rollouts. The rollouts are compared with ground truth through h^pred and h^gt and turned into a reward R, which feeds a purple Fast Weight box. (c) has two line plots, QMSum and SAMSum, showing drift against steps for DeltaNet-base, SFT, ReFINE and Transformer. The Transformer line is flat and low, and ReFINE sits below SFT.
caption: (a) Adapted from [ref]. Fast weight models replace the KV-cache in standard transformers with a recurrent fixed-size memory ($W$), updated according to [ref]. (b) Standard NTP provides token-level supervision through cross-entropy loss at each position. \ours provides sequence-level supervision by optimizing the rewards of multi-token rollouts at high-entropy positions with RL. (c) Fast weight models show larger divergence in the last layer's output representations, measured by Euclidean distance between predicted and ground truth response trajectories, than standard transformers. \ours substantially reduces this divergence compared to SFT. Error bars show $\pm 1\sigma$ across 50 independent generations.
abstract: Fast weight architectures offer a promising alternative to standard transformers for long-context modeling by replacing the KV-cache with a recurrently updated fixed-size memory. Despite this architectural shift, they are typically trained with the same next-token prediction (NTP) objective as standard transformers. This creates a mismatch: fast weight models rely on an evolving memory state to support future predictions, while NTP provides only token-level supervision for the immediate next token. We address this mismatch with next-sequence prediction (NSP), a sequence-level extension of NTP that trains models to produce coherent multi-token continuations from their recurrent memory state. To optimize this sequence-level objective, we propose ReFINE (Reinforced Fast weIghts via Next sEquence prediction). ReFINE selects informative token positions based on prediction entropy, generates multi-token rollouts, assigns sequence-level rewards, and optimizes the model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). ReFINE is applicable throughout the training lifecycle of pre-trained language models: mid-training, post-training, and test-time training. Experiments on LaCT-760M and DeltaNet-1.3B show that ReFINE consistently outperforms NTP-based supervised fine-tuning in needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, long-context question answering, and diverse tasks in LongBench. ReFINE provides an effective and versatile framework for improving long-context modeling in fast weight architectures.
